source_text: Quid igitur hic primum accusem, impudentiam mentientis, libidinem disputantis an profanitatem tam prava credentis? Nobis tamen intellego utendum Prophetae esse verbis: Beati sumus, Israel, quoniam quae Deo placent, nobis nota sunt [n254] .
pass_a_gloss: What therefore here shall I first accuse, the shamelessness of one lying, the appetite of one disputing, or the profanity of one believing so depraved things? To us nevertheless I understand the words of the Prophet must be used: We are blessed, Israel, since those things which please God are known to us.

lemmas.lexica: LS libido; Blaise often sexual desire; Julian treats as created sensation, not a sin-nature

pass_b_english: What should I accuse first here: the liar’s shamelessness, the debater’s appetite, or the irreverence of believing such perverse things? Yet I understand that we should use the prophet’s words: ‘We are blessed, Israel, because we know what pleases God’ (Baruch 4:4).

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
